hints: Differentiate both equations with respect to $\theta$, taking care that differentiating $\cos2\theta$ introduces a factor of $2$.
After dividing, replace $\sin2\theta$ by $2\sin\theta\cos\theta$ and cancel the common $\sin\theta$ factor.
Rewrite the remaining expression using $\cos\theta=1-2\sin^2(\theta/2)$ to reach the stated form.
walkthrough:
Differentiate the parametric equation $x = 1 - \cos\theta$ with respect to $\theta$:
$$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}\theta} = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\theta}(1) - \dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\theta}(\cos\theta) = 0 - (-\sin\theta) = \sin\theta$$

Differentiate the parametric equation $y = \cos\theta - \dfrac{1}{4}\cos 2\theta$ with respect to $\theta$ using the chain rule:
$$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\theta}(\cos\theta) = -\sin\theta$$
$$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\theta}\left(-\dfrac{1}{4}\cos 2\theta\right) = -\dfrac{1}{4}(-2\sin 2\theta) = +\dfrac{1}{2}\sin 2\theta$$
Combine the terms:
$$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}\theta} = -\sin\theta + \dfrac{1}{2}\sin 2\theta$$

Use the double-angle identity $\sin 2\theta = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta$ in the numerator:
$$\dfrac{1}{2}\sin 2\theta = \dfrac{1}{2}(2\sin\theta\cos\theta) = \sin\theta\cos\theta$$
The expression becomes:
$$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{-\sin\theta + \sin\theta\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}$$

Factor out $\sin\theta$ from the numerator and cancel the common factor $\sin\theta$:
$$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{\sin\theta(-1 + \cos\theta)}{\sin\theta} = \cos\theta - 1$$

Conclude that the derivative is in the required form:
$$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = -2\sin^2\!\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\theta\right)$$
